Q: global variables between modules/files and functions A:

You need to store this value somewhere else, like a key-value store or a database.

The approach you show here has two problems. If the Web server ever restarts (maybe you run out of memory or your server crashed or you just need to upgrade the code) you lose the value of the global variable. If you have enough load that you need to run multiple copies of the server, they won't share the global variable, and the response a client will get will be random depending on which server it happens to hit.

More generally, using global variables and the global keyword leads to code that's hard to test and can have concurrency problems. What happens if your service receives multiple concurrent requests to the "calculate" endpoint, and the asyncio operation suspends and resumes in the middle of the call; is it possible one of the increments will be lost, or with the code as you've written it, you'll have two concurrent loops both incrementing the variable and the value will wind up twice as high as you expect?

I'd consider this a strong enough anti-pattern that I wouldn't worry about getting the import semantics right. Refactor this to be concurrency-safe and remove the global variable entirely.

Q: Mobile Optimization and Removing Active Content for eBay Listing Description A:

Pop-ups will not work in an eBay listing because eBay blocks all “active content” such as JavaScript, scripts, iframes, and pop-up functionality under its active content policy, so links must remain simple standard hyperlinks. The issue with the image not scaling on mobile is likely because the image does not have responsive styling and the table layout includes large spacing that breaks the layout on smaller screens. To fix this, remove large table spacing and make the image responsive by adding inline CSS such as style="max-width:100%; height:auto;", which allows the image to automatically scale to the width of the device screen. Simplifying the layout and using basic HTML with minimal tables and inline CSS will make the description display properly on both desktop and mobile while remaining fully compliant with eBay’s policies.

Q: Best practices for thread-safe collections API? A:

The best practice in parallel/high-performance codes is not to use such data structure at all. They do not scale on many-cores CPUs and are not flexible enough. On concurrent codes (where performance is not critical) scalability is often not critical so this one is not an issue, but flexibility still is. The main issue is that the best choice for locks is dependent of the algorithm. Using a global lock for all the methods provided by the data-structure is often enough in complex cases. For exemple, you cannot add an entry in an hash-map depending on the existence of another one in a thread-safe way without using another lock on the user-side. Adding a new lock this way cause the one in the data structure to be useless: all access to the data structure now needs to be protected with the user lock. While you can expose the lock to the user, I do not see any benefit compared to just using a lock on the user side and use a standard data structure without an internal lock (which require more memory and impacting performance when used for no reason). Fine grain locking can be useful in some pretty-specific use-case for some data structure since the user cannot implement that easily, but people often reimplement them due to the lack of flexibility/performance of the generic thread-safe (or atomic) data structure.

Regarding spin locks, I strongly encourage not to use them. They can be very harmful. It is a bad idea to use them when you have no full control of the target machine (i.e. not owned by you) or if you can prove it will not spin more than few iterations (i.e. bounded to a low value) before using system locks. They can cause sneaky hard-to-reproduce deadlocks due to priority inversion on some platforms (e.g. PS4/PS5 and some Linux systems due to a different scheduler). They tend to increase the energy consumption (PState/CState switches and even causes mad frequency boosts) which is critical on laptop/mobile/low-power devices. It can also decrease performance of other applications on the user machine by preventing useful context-switches or by confusing scheduling stacks (see Intel Thread Director on modern Intel CPUs). In fact, Intel advise not to use them as well as Linus did too. To quote him:

Do not use spinlocks in user space, unless you actually know what you're doing. And be aware that the likelihood that you know what you are doing is basically nil.

Thus, except in few niche use-cases, spin-locks must be combined with locks (i.e. adaptative spin-locks) or not used at all.
